newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica, EU headed for showdown on free trade deal.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica, EU headed for showdown on free trade deal.

text.p: South Africa and the European Union (EU) are heading for a showdown in coming months when they return to the negotiating table with widely differing views on the nature and timing of a free trade deal.
In recent weeks the EU mandate for negotiations has been criticised as too harsh by a number of influential parties in South Africa and its neighbouring countries.
The EU has refused post-apartheid South Africa full accession to the Lome Convention which grants favourable access to its markets to developing countries in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific.

Instead the European Commission wants to exclude up to 40 percent of South Africa's agricultural products, including wine and citrus fruits, while calling on the developing country to extensively reduce tariffs to ensure easier access to its market for European producers.
South African parliamentarians late last month said the EU offer failed to take account of the very different sizes and levels of development of the economies of the negotiating partners.

"(The) EU proposal would have the effect of requiring of South Africa rather severe adjustment costs to secure only modest additional duty-free access to the EU," a report from the parliamentary committees on agriculture, trade and industry and foreign affairs said.

South Africa's four closest neighbours -- Botswana, Lesotho, Namibia and Swaziland -- which are linked together in the common monetary area of the Southern African Customs Union, fear heavy losses in customs revenue if the EU's call for extensive tariff reductions is heeded.
This week they asked the South African parliament to consult with their parliaments before accepting a negotiating mandate.

Preliminary studies by the Namibian Economic Policy Research Unit indicate the free trade agreement could slash the customs union's revenue by between N$1.3 billion ($290 million) and N$3.5 billion a year. The research body did not give figures for total customs revenue.

Jayendra Naidoo, executive director of the National Economic, Development and Labour Council (Nedlac) which is assessing the impact on South Africa of the EU offer said the general response was one of disappointment.

"(The) offer was much more hardnosed than the one that was expected...The South African economy is being opened up on its weak spots and the European economy is being protected in the areas where we can actually advance," Naidoo told Reuters.

The EU for its part is getting restless waiting for South Africa to respond to its mandate which has been on the table since March. It has already warned South Africa that the opportunity for a free trade deal might not exist indefinitely.
A European Commission spokesman in Brussels this week told Reuters he hoped South Africa would be able to respond to the EU's mandate in October, with a deal following soon afterwards.
"We are eager to negotiate. We want an agreement in place by early next year to coincide with the entry into force of the new Lome convention," the spokesman said.
But South African observers to the talks do not expect a deal to be signed for many months, even years, although its negotiating mandate was expected to be ready by the end of October.

"There is a period of negotiation coming up, definitely. It is not a time to go with a pen in hand and sign. I am surprised to hear...that they (the EU) are expecting to finish by the end of this year," said Nedlac's Naidoo.

Rob Davies, acting chairman of parliament's committee on trade and industry, said: "Some people involved in the discussions say a year or two even...Getting the thing right, is the most important thing."
But although a rocky path of negotiations lie ahead observers remain confident South Africa will strike a beneficial deal.

"It is too important (for South Africa) for there not to be an agreement. Europe is our largest trading partner by a long way," said Antoinette Handley, the director of studies at the Institute of International Affairs.
Some forty percent of South Africa's exports go to EU member states, and more than one third of its imports are EU in origin.
"The (EU) mandate is simply that. It is not set in stone and is just a starting point for negotiations," she said. ($1 =
